## Overview

This project builds a search engine over a corpus of arXiv malware-classification
papers, implementing and comparing six retrieval methods head-to-head:
**BM25 → dense (SPECTER2) → hybrid (RRF) → cross-encoder rerank → late-interaction
(ColBERT via Qdrant) → generative retrieval (a trained query→semantic-ID model)**.

Every method is evaluated on the same 40-query, LLM-judged relevance-labeled
eval set, using the same NDCG@10 / MRR metrics, and benchmarked on the same
latency harness. The goal was not just to build each technique, but to
honestly report where each one wins, where it loses, and why — including
findings that didn't come out the way theory alone would predict.

Code: [github.com/vinayhpandya/search-algorithms](https://github.com/vinayhpandya/search-algorithms)

## Corpus and Setup

- **Domain**: arXiv papers on malware classification (`cs.CR`, `cs.LG`, `cs.CV`
  categories), collected via the `arxiv` client library across 16 search
  queries, deduplicated
- **Enrichment**: citation counts from Semantic Scholar (used later as an
  LTR feature)
- **Index**: OpenSearch, single-node local Docker setup — chosen because it
  supports BM25 and k-NN vector search natively in one engine, letting
  lexical and semantic search share the same index and fuse without
  cross-system round trips
- **Scope decision**: abstract-only (no full-text PDFs), to keep the repo
  small and the project achievable in a weekend — noted as future work

## Methodology: Evaluation

### Relevance labeling

Manually labeling enough query-paper pairs for a meaningful eval set (857
pairs across 40 queries at initial scope, growing further as more methods
were added) isn't realistic by hand in the available time. Instead:

1. A **researcher** LLM rates each pair 0/1/2 with a rationale
2. A **critic** LLM reviews the researcher's rating and either confirms or
   overrides it — final label = critic's call
3. A **human spot-check** on a stratified sample (~65 pairs, weighted toward
   researcher/critic disagreements) validates the LLM labels

This is standard practice for evaluating relevance judgments at scale (the
same logic behind TREC-style IR evaluation and industry search-quality
teams checking LLM/crowd-worker judgments) — not a shortcut.

**Known calibration issue**: only ~3% of labeled pairs were rated "not
relevant" (0). Because candidate pools are built from real search results
(already topically adjacent to the query), the researcher/critic prompts
turned out lenient about what counts as irrelevant. This doesn't invalidate
the labels — NDCG@10 still discriminates well since it weights label=2 three
times as heavily as label=1 — but it does mean **MRR at the standard
threshold (label ≥ 1) saturates near 1.0 for every method** and carries no
signal. Reporting **MRR at threshold ≥ 2** ("how often is the very best
result found immediately") restored real discrimination between methods
without needing to relabel anything.

### Metrics

- **NDCG@10**: rewards ranking highly-relevant results near the top;
  uses the full graded (0/1/2) label
- **MRR(≥2)**: reciprocal rank of the first *highly* relevant result — the
  metric that actually discriminates given this corpus's label distribution
- **Latency**: mean / p50 / p95 across 40 queries × 5 runs each (first run
  per query discarded as warmup), local machine, no GPU

## Results: Retrieval Quality

| Method | NDCG@10 | MRR(≥1) | MRR(≥2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| BM25             | 0.9003 | 1.0000 | 0.5969 |
| Dense            | 0.9026 | 1.0000 | 0.5763 |
| Hybrid           | 0.9142 | 1.0000 | 0.7261 |
| Rerank           | 0.9131 | 1.0000 | 0.7504 |
| Late-interaction | 0.9003 | 1.0000 | 0.6951 |
| Semantic ID (generative) | 0.9624 | 0.9625 | 0.2744 |

### Reading the core four methods

**Dense underperforms BM25 on MRR(≥2)** (0.5763 vs 0.5969) despite
near-identical NDCG@10 — SPECTER2 embeddings surface broadly topical
neighbors well, but are less precise than exact keyword matching at
pinpointing the single best match at rank 1.

**Hybrid and rerank both correct for this**, each clearly outperforming
either input alone on MRR(≥2) — real evidence of fusion and reranking doing
genuine work, not just reshuffling noise.

**Late-interaction lands between dense and hybrid** (MRR≥2 = 0.6951) —
consistent with the theoretical expectation that token-level (MaxSim)
matching captures finer-grained relevance than single-vector cosine
similarity, without needing full cross-attention.

**Rerank is the best quality by both metrics** — expected, since a
cross-encoder sees the full query and document jointly via cross-attention
(strictly more expressive than any similarity-metric-based method here),
at the cost of only being feasible on a pre-filtered shortlist, never the
whole corpus.

### The semantic ID result

At face value, the generative retrieval method's NDCG@10 (0.9624) is the
*highest* of all six methods — but this is a labeling artifact, not a
genuine quality win, and the MRR(≥2) column makes that clear (0.2744, by
far the *lowest* of all six).

The trained query→semantic-ID model (t5-small, fine-tuned on ~660 synthetic
query examples) suffered **mode collapse**: it predicts the same coarse/fine
cluster (`[1, 0]`) for a large share of unrelated queries, rather than
genuinely discriminating between them (see sample predictions below). That
cluster happens to be a large, generically-malware-relevant group of
papers — so almost any malware-related query retrieves *something*
"somewhat relevant" from it (driving MRR(≥1) and NDCG up), but essentially
never the *single best* paper for a specific query (driving MRR(≥2) down).
This is a coherent, honest finding: **the model learned to be right about
the wrong thing** — a shortcut that scores deceptively well on a lenient
metric while providing near-zero real retrieval discrimination.
